about: Every setting of a project's file (hive/projects/<project>.json), as tools/hive/hive.py reads it: one entry for each, and no other. 'required': the file must give it; otherwise 'default' is what the hive takes when the file says nothing. 'least' and 'most' are bounds the hive enforces when it loads the file (a file outside them does not load); a setting without them is not bounded there. 'fixed': the one value the hive takes. A test of the hive (tools/hive/test_hive.py, TestTheSettingsList) holds this list to the code: neither changes alone.

presets.about: Recommended values for three ways of opening a project, whatever its judge. They are recommendations: a project's lead may change any of them, within the bounds. A setting that names no value for a way of opening keeps its default. A value written {"ask": ..., "accounts": ...} is a list of GitHub account numbers that only the lead can give ('one': exactly one; 'some': one or more). Guardians are not part of a preset: a project names them where its judge gives a figure they may waive (guardians.accounts), and members.per_guardian then has its own recommendations.
presets.trial: One account, the project lead's own, to try the whole pipeline: no wait, many deals a day.
presets.invitation: A pilot: the accounts the lead names, the hive's ordinary pace.
presets.open: Open to any GitHub account old enough, at the hive's ordinary pace.

types.protocol: the version of the hive's protocol, a whole number
types.branch: a branch's own name, with no refs/ or heads/ in front
types.accounts: a list of GitHub account numbers
types.accounts or none: a list of GitHub account numbers, or null
types.accounts and logins: a list of GitHub account numbers; a login is taken too
types.models: a list of model identifiers (letters, digits, dots, dashes and underscores, no space)
types.judge kind: one of the kinds of judge the hive holds: common, reference
types.commits: a list of full commit ids
types.figures: a list of names of the judge's figures
types.conditions: a list of conditions on kept figures: {name, min or max, and optionally and: [conditions]}
types.waivers: figures, each with the most a guardian's ruling may let it reach
types.patterns: a list of paths or path patterns (dir/** for everything below a folder): printable, relative, with no empty or dot part

settings.what: The version of the hive's protocol the file is written for. A file that names another does not load.
The project's name in the hive: lower-case letters, digits and hyphens. It is also the name of its file and of its state folder: a file whose project is not its own name does not load.
The GitHub repository the hive reads and writes for this project.
The branch the hive writes: what its judge accepted, one commit per task. Never the branch the project publishes: a file that names one branch for both does not load.
The branch people take the project from. The hive never writes it: the project's maintainers move it to what they have read.
Where the project's tasks are listed: one place, which bears the project's name.
The project's own quick check: one command line a worker runs in the project's sandbox before it submits. Empty: the project has none.
True stops every step of the hive for this project: nothing is read, dealt, judged or written.

Null: any account that meets the other rules may work. A list: only these accounts, by GitHub account number (a number survives a change of login). A file that names one account alone is a trial: it may ask no wait, and its one account, named guardian too, may admit a commit of its own.
How old a GitHub account must be for the hive to read its fork as a member's: accounts made for the occasion wait.

Accounts whose forks the hive does not read, and whose work no guardian's ruling brings in. Ban by number: a number is the same everywhere, and a login can change hands. An account the file bans by number is never one of its guardians: a file that names it both does not load.
Whether the hive follows, when its rules lose nothing by it, the part of the project a member's worker says it prefers.
The models the project keeps statistics for; a worker that declares another is recorded as undeclared.

The accounts the project trusts, by GitHub account number, each once, one at least; never one the file bans. A guardian decides alone and at once, in public, on one named commit; it holds no key. A project names guardians where its judge gives a figure it requires by a single maximum (judge.metrics and judge.require), together with what they may waive (guardians.waive); or it names neither, and takes no ruling.

The figures a guardian may let go for one commit, and how far, one at least: only a figure the project keeps and requires by a single maximum, with a bound that is that maximum at least. The commit is judged again in full, that figure aside. Given together with guardians.accounts, or not at all.

How many active members one guardian covers. Beyond guardians times this number, the hive deals no task to a new member; those that are active go on. Null: no such bound. A file that sets it without naming a guardian does not load; where a project names guardians, the recommendations are its own (not those of a trial, which has one account).
A member is active while it holds a task, and for this many days after each candidate of its own that the project accepted.
How long a member has to push its candidate once a task is dealt to it.
How long after that the hive still waits before the deal runs out.

The wait after a deal that ended without an accepted candidate: this wait, each time, after a candidate the judge examined and refused; after a deal left without a candidate or a candidate refused before the judge, this wait doubled at each such deal in a row, seven days at most. A candidate short of a proof alone costs none, nor does an ending of the hive's or the project's doing; an acceptance clears it. An hour at least; none at all (0) only while the file names one account alone as its members.
How many tasks an account may be dealt in a day, those whose candidate was accepted left out.
The most lines a candidate may change.
The most files a candidate may change.
The largest file a candidate may leave changed, or bring in any of its own commits. A file the project already had may grow to twice what it was, if that is more.
The longest line a candidate may add.
The most commits a candidate may add to the project's history.
What a candidate's own commits may weigh together, as git packs them on the project's tip. One fetch of a fork writes four times this at most.
How many new branch tips of one fork the hive reads in a run; a fork with more is not read until it has fewer.
How many candidates one run judges; the others wait for the next, oldest deal first.
How long a run spends reading forks; those it has not reached wait for the next run.
How long a run spends judging: no judgement is started that could end after it.
How many candidates a plan lists at most.

How a candidate is found right. common: outputs identical to the base, and measures taken beside it (a faster or smaller same thing). reference: the unit a task names answers exactly as the project's reference does (a port, a rewrite).
common judge: how many times each measure is taken.
The longest one judgement may take.
common judge: options handed to the project's own plug-in; a task may add its own.
Commits of the project's own history its judge reads by id (a corpus as the project had it, for instance): full ids, sixteen at most.
The judge's figures the hive keeps on a verdict's line. A goal, a requirement, a proof or a waiver can only name one of these.
The judge's proofs the project takes: kept figures named sure_<measure>, those the judged program cannot bear upon. Every goal on a figure must hold one.
What the project requires of every contribution, whatever its task: conditions on kept figures. They can only refuse.

Paths no candidate may change, beside those the hive protects in every project ('always': the hive's own folder at the root, and, at any depth and in any letter case, the names and folders that steer git, CI and editors, and that coding agents read as instructions). The project's own sandbox, judge and tests are not among them: a project's file lists them here.

not_settings: Where project code runs (the project's sandbox, the judge's containers, without network) is the hive's, the same for every project: no project file changes it.
What a member may write (branches of its own fork, nothing else) and what the hive keeps of a fork's text (nothing) are the hive's.
The hive's own code and the commit of it that runs are the registry's: a project's file names a kind of judge, never brings one.
What is protected in every project (the 'always' of the protected setting): a project's file adds paths to these; it removes none.

The hive's own counts: three failures that are a candidate's own before it is refused, six runs without an answer before a deal is closed at no cost, a day for a fork that could not be read, a wait that doubles up to seven days.

The hive's own bounds on what a run does besides a project's limits, which have bounds of their own: the branches it lists of one fork, what all the fetches of a run leave, what a plan carries to the other steps, how long it weighs candidates.
A project's tasks are a file of their own (hive/tasks/<project>.jsonl); a task says its files, its tier, its goal and its options there, not in the project's file.
